target: Animal dissection is valuable because it improves learning opportunities, critical thinking, and practical biology skills.
objection: Real-animal dissection is ethically and environmentally problematic because the animals are supplied through inhumane methods and, according to AG2, most dissection animals are caught in the wild, which harms local populations and biodiversity.

target: Animal dissection is justified because it is not required by AP Biology, NGSS, or medical training.
objection: Dissection is unnecessary for science or medical education because it is not required by College Board AP Biology or the Next Generation Science Standards, and no U.S. or Canadian medical schools use animals to train physicians.

target: Animal dissection is justified because there are no equally good substitutes.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach as well as or better than real-animal dissection, so alternatives can provide comparable or superior learning outcomes without using dead animals.

target: The fact that dissection is not explicitly required by AP Biology or NGSS means it should be rejected as an instructional method.
objection: Education standards set learning objectives and investigation practices; they do not prohibit specific lab methods, so a method can still be appropriate if it helps students meet those objectives.

target: Alternatives can be assumed to teach internal anatomy just as well as real dissection.
objection: Real dissection gives students direct specimen-based observation of true 3D anatomical relationships and real tissue characteristics, while synthetic models and simulations are only approximations that cannot fully reproduce those features.

target: Dissection is unnecessary because medical training does not use it.
objection: School biology education has goals that are different from physician training, so a method can be valuable for school biology even if it is not used in medical education.

target: Typical school dissection uses already-dead byproduct specimens, so it does not depend on wild-capturing animals.
objection: If most dissection animals are caught in the wild, then dissection programs typically rely on live-captured animals rather than only already-dead meat-industry byproducts.

target: Dissection is educationally valuable because it creates hands-on “aha moments,” and because it is not required for physician training it should still be allowed in school biology.
objection: Hands-on dissection can inspire enthusiasm for science and careers in science, so dissection can be worthwhile in biology classes even if it is not medically required.

target: Alternatives can be assumed to provide the same critical-thinking opportunities as real dissection.
objection: Real anatomical specimens present natural variability and unanticipated differences that students must interpret, so dissection uniquely fosters deeper critical thinking than simplified models or simulations.

target: The ethical objection still applies even when specimens are already-dead byproducts.
objection: If the specimens are already-dead meat-industry byproducts, dissection does not usually require collecting live wild animals, so the claimed wild-population and biodiversity harms do not typically arise in the byproduct scenario.

target: Alternatives can be assumed to provide the same tactile, procedure-based anatomy learning as real dissection.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations are only approximations and do not necessarily reproduce the tactile properties of real tissue or the manual procedures involved in dissecting real specimens.

target: Fine-motor and hand-eye-coordination benefits do not justify real-animal dissection.
objection: Dissection develops fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination, and those are important educational outcomes for hands-on biology lab work; alternatives usually do not fully replicate that manual tissue-handling practice.

target: Alternatives cannot provide dissection-equivalent manual tissue-handling practice.
objection: Classroom alternatives such as tactile simulators and synthetic tissue-like anatomy models can let students manually cut and handle materials to expose structures, so they can provide comparable fine-motor and hand-eye-coordination practice.

target: Dissection is unnecessary because alternatives can generate primary data just as well.
objection: Biology curricula emphasize scientific investigation through direct observation of specimens, and dissection lets students collect first-hand, specimen-based evidence rather than only viewing predetermined visuals or data.

target: Alternatives cannot provide specimen-based evidence comparable to dissection.
objection: Educational virtual dissection software and 3D synthetic anatomy platforms can let students manipulate specimens and record quantitative or structured observations, so they can generate primary, specimen-based evidence in ways comparable to real dissection.

target: Most dissection specimens come from wild-capture, so dissection unavoidably causes biodiversity harm.
objection: If over 98% of dissected animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, then typical school dissection does not depend on wild-captured animals and does not unavoidably create the biodiversity harms claimed.

target: Typical school dissection specimens are already-dead byproducts rather than wild-captured animals.
objection: If approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, then dissection supply chains are overwhelmingly based on live-capture/wild-catching rather than exclusively on already-dead meat-industry byproducts.

target: Dissection should be rejected because it produces no special educational value beyond alternatives and harms biodiversity.
objection: Real dissection offers hands-on observation of real anatomical variability, practical skill-building, and engagement benefits that alternatives cannot be assumed to fully match; in the usual byproduct-supply scenario, the ethical downside is reduced.

target: The educational benefits of dissection require real animals.
objection: The benefits AG1 cites—hands-on observation, critical thinking, engagement, and manual practice—can be obtained with synthetic models and alternative dissection labs without using real animals.

target: Real-animal dissection is unnecessary because alternatives can match all the same learning outcomes.
objection: Real specimens provide direct tactile and procedural experience with real tissue properties and anatomical variability that models and simulations cannot be assumed to fully replicate, so the learning benefits are not necessarily interchangeable.

target: Typical school dissection uses already-dead byproducts rather than wild-caught animals.
objection: Dissection specimens that come from the meat industry still come from an inhumane and environmentally harmful supply chain, so using byproducts does not eliminate the ethical and environmental problems of real-animal dissection.

target: Real-animal dissection remains objectionable even when using already-dead byproducts.
objection: Using animals that were already dead and destined for landfill is a productive use of dead material and reduces the ethical downside compared with using live animals specifically for teaching.

target: Dissection is acceptable if it uses already-dead byproducts and provides educational value.
objection: Because the supply chain is still dominated by wild-capture, school dissection typically still carries the biodiversity harms associated with capture-based sourcing rather than only using already-dead byproducts.

target: Real-animal dissection should be retained because alternatives may not fully replicate tactile/procedural learning and engagement.
objection: Alternatives may support some learning, but they cannot be assumed to fully replace the tactile, procedural, and real-anatomical-variability experiences of dissection.

target: Alternatives cannot be assumed to match real dissection’s tactile/procedural and variability-based learning outcomes.
objection: If alternatives deliver comparable biology learning outcomes, then they can also deliver the relevant tactile, procedural, and variability-based outcomes that dissection is used to teach.

target: Dissection should be recommended when it helps meet AP/NGSS learning goals and uses already-dead byproducts.
objection: School biology standards emphasize hands-on learning goals such as fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and science engagement, and dissection can satisfy those goals; if alternatives are not shown to match them without killing animals, dissection remains justified in the byproduct scenario.

target: Dissection should be used whenever alternatives are not proven to match the same outcomes.
objection: Alternatives already teach as well or better for the relevant biology goals, and since AP Biology and NGSS do not require animal dissection, the ethical and environmental harms of dissection are not justified when alternatives are available.
